Document Title: MCP-based AI coding agent Integrating Static Analysis for Web Accessibility Error Correction
Authors: Y. Higuchi; J. -E. Kim; M. Bessho
Author Affiliations: Faculty of Information Networking for Innovation and Design, Toyo University, Tokyo, Japan; Department of Information Networking for Innovation and Design, Toyo University, Tokyo, Japan; Department of Information Networking for Innovation and Design, Toyo University, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract: While ensuring web accessibility is becoming a legal obligation, 94.8% of the top one million websites violate WCAG standards, highlighting the need for more efficient implementation support in development environments. This paper proposes a novel approach to ensuring web accessibility using general-purpose AI coding agents by providing them with appropriate contextual information for accessibility error correction through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This approach enables integration of Biome’s static analysis with the flexible code-base understanding capabilities of AI coding agents to efficiently produce WCAG-compliant fixes. Adopting the MCP architecture enables uniform use across various AI coding agent environments, such as Claude Code and Roo Code. We conducted experiments using an AI coding agent with four different LLM backends on a common test case and demonstrated the feasibility of our approach.

Document Title: Evolution Context Gap: An Empirical Study of Agent Manifests
Authors: N. Chondamrongkul; W. Rueangsirarak; P. Jakkaew
Author Affiliations: School of Applied Digital Technology, Mae Fah Luang University, Chiang Rai, Thailand; School of Applied Digital Technology, Mae Fah Luang University, Chiang Rai, Thailand; School of Applied Digital Technology, Mae Fah Luang University, Chiang Rai, Thailand
Publication Title: 2026 23rd International Joint Conference on Computer Science and Software Engineering (JCSSE)
Abstract: AI coding agents—Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor—increasingly rely on developer-authored instruction les (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, etc.) to understand project context. These agent manifests have not been systematically studied. We present the first large-scale content analysis of 80 real-world manifests drawn from five agent types using a six-category taxonomy and a three-model LLM classifier with majority-vote consensus. Workflow & Process dominates (present in 96.2% of manifests, 43.5% mean character fraction), while evolution context—information about how the software changes over time—is largely absent: 73.8% of manifests contain no evolution content, and none references Lehman’s laws of software evolution. A single significant project-level correlation emerges: manifests in more law-conformant projects contain more coding-style guidance (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.040, n=23). These findings characterise a systematic evolution context gap that leaves agents architecture-blind and motivate automated manifest enrichment tooling.

Document Title: Execution Control Harness for Governed LLM-Based Code Generation
Authors: M. Takeda; Y. Funaya; O. Harriet; R. Mibe; H. Kanuka
Author Affiliations: Digital Infrastructure Innovation Center, Research & Development Group, Hitachi, Ltd., Tokyo, Japan; Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation Center, Research & Development Group, Hitachi, Ltd., Tokyo, Japan; Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation Center, Research & Development Group, Hitachi, Ltd., Tokyo, Japan; Systems Innovation Center, Research & Development Group, Hitachi, Ltd., Yokohama, Japan; Systems Innovation Center, Research & Development Group, Hitachi, Ltd., Yokohama, Japan
Publication Title: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
Abstract: LLM-based coding agents have strong potential for automating software development, but their direct application remains fragile under long and complex requirements. Specification omissions are common, and autonomous local fixes can trigger cascading regressions. In a preliminary experiment, implementing a single business function using a standard specification-driven approach required 65 interaction rounds and approximately 9 hours of manual correction.In this paper, we propose an execution control harness that tightly couples LLM-based code generation with governed execution. Implemented as a YAML-based workflow DSL, the harness integrates mechanically scoped reasoning, deterministic validation gates, automated Git-based rollback, and hybrid human-agent control.A case study on a real-world insurance application of approximately 30 KLOC suggests that the proposed approach helps suppress specification omissions and regression chains. Under comparable conditions, the number of correction iterations was reduced from 65 to 3, and total development time decreased from 9.0 to 0.5 hours. These results indicate that reliable AI-driven software development requires not only capable agents but also execution control architectures that govern the generation process.

Document Title: GHAgentFiles: A dataset of coding agent file histories in GitHub repositories
Authors: G. Cardoen; T. Mens; A. Decan
Author Affiliations: Software Engineering Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium; Software Engineering Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium; Software Engineering Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium
Publication Title: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
Abstract: Since the introduction of coding-specific LLMs in the early 2020s, coding agents have become increasingly popular in collaborative software development projects. Since 2025, it is common practice to specify context files that provide additional context to coding agents about the project structure, development commands, coding conventions, and so on. To enable large-scale empirical studies of collaborative GitHub repositories involving coding agents, we provide a dataset of context, skill and subagent files and an open-source tool to identify and extract such files automatically. Out of an initial list of 165K+ repositories, we identify 27K+ repositories with coding agent files for six major agents (Claude, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Windsurf and Cursor), resulting in 142K+ distinct file histories and 401K+ revisions covering their evolution. We conduct a preliminary observational analysis on this large dataset and present some perspectives to the research community on how to use this dataset for future empirical studies.

Author Affiliations: Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence, Federal University of Goiás, Goiás, Brazil; Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence, Federal University of Goiás, Goiás, Brazil; Information Systems, Federal University of Mato Grosso do Sul, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil; Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence, Federal University of Goiás, Goiás, Brazil; Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence, Federal University of Goiás, Goiás, Brazil

Abstract: AI coding assistants are transforming software development, but most approaches remain code-centric and weakly connected to requirements, specifications, architectural decisions, organizational standards, and quality gates. This paper presents Spec-Driven AI, a multiagent framework for specification-centric Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) automation. The framework combines an SDLC orchestrator, specialized lifecycle agents, human-in-the-loop gates, auditable artifact generation, and a Pattern Manager / Context Platform that provides governed context through repository indexing, document retrieval, knowledge graph extraction, adherence validation, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. Spec-Driven AI treats specifications as verifiable contracts and uses agents to coordinate discovery, specification, design, planning, implementation support, testing, review, and traceability. We describe the architecture, implementation, and demonstration scenario showing how a project is registered, indexed, governed, and used to prepare structured context for SDLC agents. Document Title: A Knowledge Engineering Framework for AI-Driven Software Development: Harness, Guardrail, and AI-Native Knowledge DevOps
Authors: K. Watanabe; H. Ogawa; S. Ito; T. Nakazawa; K. Tsuru
Author Affiliations: Digital Innovation R&D, Hitachi, Ltd., Japan; Digital Innovation R&D, Hitachi, Ltd., Japan; Digital Innovation R&D, Hitachi, Ltd., Japan; Digital Innovation R&D, Hitachi, Ltd., Japan; Digital Innovation R&D, Hitachi, Ltd., Japan
Publication Title: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
Abstract: Development-time knowledge—design rationale, architectural decisions, domain constraints, hard-won lessons—generated during AI-driven software development is largely ephemeral, lost between agent sessions. We propose a knowledge engineering framework whose guiding principle is pervasive AI participation—an aspirational design stance in which the agent accompanies the development workflow as broadly as practical and externalizes what it observes into machine-readable artifacts. The framework casts an Effective Agent as Foundation Model + (Harness ∥ Guardrail): two parallel operational concerns—Harness (course-setting; Knowledge, Skills, Stakeholder personas, Runtime/loader) and Guardrail (deviation detection; static analysis, automated tests, an adversarial review-gate drawing on a heterogeneous foundation-model family (untested), post-push review). A separate, external meta-process, AI-Native Knowledge DevOps (Capture/Refine/Create/Apply, GitOps-versioned, agent-loop driven), refines them across sessions: capture Guardrail findings and re-inject refined artifacts into both Harness and Guardrail. Adopting ADRs, GitOps, and concurrent harness-engineering corpora (AGENTS.md, plans, post-integration sensors, AI-rule promotion [1]–[3]) as foundations rather than novelty, our narrower contribution is a four-cell Harness, a Guardrail panel at parity, and a dual-target refinement loop (a design hypothesis we present, not an evaluated effect). A 142-day, 297-commit longitudinal experience report (a marketsizing tool for business planning under the TAM/SAM/SOM framework, built with Claude Code plus an OpenAI Codex CLI review-gate) illustrates the framework: 9,441 LOC, 441 tests, 14 knowledge documents (7,349 lines), and 92 issues (78 filed via the agent’s issue-lifecycle Skill). Commit-history analysis shows 63% of commits on the agent-loaded artifacts are maintenance-class rather than purely additive—we report this as a descriptive number, not as evidence the cycle caused the share, since the case is N=1 with the developer overlapping the framework authors.
Author Keywords: knowledge engineering;AI-driven software development;LLM coding agents;knowledge DevOps;harness engineering
